lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Question You Did Not Expect

listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to the second day of the Cross-Border Counsel Forum. My name is Ruth and I chair the programme committee. Three things before we start. The keynote has moved to the main hall at half past nine, because the room we booked yesterday was far too small, and I am told it was standing room only. The afternoon runs in three parallel panels, and the one on compliance in Latin America has already filled up, so please register at the desk if you have not done that yet. Finally, the delegate list is now on the app, with everybody's employer and city. If you have come here to meet your counterpart in another country, this is the morning to do it. Coffee is outside, and we start in twenty minutes.

The hardest question at any conference is not a legal one. It is: so, what did you think? And I have watched very competent people go completely blank on it, in their own language. Here is what I tell junior lawyers. Do not try to summarise the whole day. Pick one thing. Say what it was, say why it stayed with you, and say what you would do differently on Monday because of it. Thirty seconds, three moves. If you genuinely have nothing, be honest and turn the question round: name the session you are still thinking about, and ask what struck them. Nobody has ever minded that. The people who sound impressive at these events are not the ones with the most to say. They are the ones who decided, before they walked in, that one clear point beats four vague ones.

extra_audio.text: Claire asks Pedro what brought him so far for a two-day conference. He explains that his company is opening an office in the United States and that he has spent six months drafting contracts in English. She says that she has been in-house counsel at an energy group for four years. She asks him what has struck him most so far, and he names the keynote. She recommends the panel after lunch, because her counterpart in Chicago is on it.
